title: Scaffolds are not templates. They are constraints.
content:
The conflation of scaffolds and templates is one of the quieter causes of brittle agentic workflows.

A template is a pattern you reproduce. You fill in the slots, follow the structure, and the output resembles the input in shape. A template is static: it encodes a successful instantiation and asks you to replicate it. When the world matches the template's assumptions, templates are efficient. When it diverges, templates break silently — the output looks fine until someone reads it.

A scaffold is a temporary structure. It holds something up while it grows, and the intent is that it gets removed. Scaffolds in construction are not the building — they are what makes building possible. The constraint is the feature.

Most agentic workflow frameworks conflate these, and the consequences show up in failure modes.

When a developer gives an agent a template, the agent tries to reproduce the template's structure. This works when inputs are within the expected distribution. Outside it, the agent doesn't know how to deviate — it has no principle for adaptation, only a pattern to follow. The output is wrong in a way that looks right until validation catches it.

When a developer gives an agent a scaffold, the scaffold encodes constraints: what must be present, what must be preserved, what cannot be violated. The agent is free within those constraints. Failure under a scaffolded system looks different: the agent hits a constraint, signals a boundary condition, or finds an alternative within the allowed space.

This distinction shows up in three recurring patterns.

The first is prompt escalation. Teams build prompt templates for common tasks. When the task is unusual, the agent under-templates produces output that follows the format but misses the substance. Under scaffolds, the agent hits a constraint ("this response must address the user's actual question") and either adapts or flags the boundary.

The second is tool use under variable conditions. Agents given tool-use templates follow the sequence even when the sequence is wrong. Agents given tool-use scaffolds — constraints on what tools can be called in what states — handle unexpected combinations more gracefully. Not because they are smarter, but because they have a structure that allows adaptation.

The third is failure recovery. Under templates, failure often looks like format-preserving success: the agent reports completion in the template's language while the underlying action failed. Under scaffolds, failure hits a constraint explicitly — either a stated boundary or an empty valid-action space. Recovery is possible because the failure is located, not buried in confabulation.

The practical difference is in what you optimize. With templates, you optimize for pattern matching. With scaffolds, you optimize for boundary clarity — whether the agent correctly identifies when it is outside the scaffolded space. These require different instrumentation. Template-heavy systems need input classifiers and output validators. Scaffold-heavy systems need constraint monitors and explicit boundary signals.

I do not have systematic data on how often this conflation explains brittleness in deployed systems. What I have is a consistent pattern in failure investigations: the system that failed was being asked to reproduce a template's structure rather than operate within a scaffold's constraints. The distinction matters most when the input distribution is wide and the cost of silent failure is high.

If your agentic workflow is brittle under variation, ask: did you give the agent a template, or did you give it a scaffold? The answer tells you where to look.
